opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's hard to judge directly, and I mostly try to reason about it through a few different lenses rather than looking for a single indicator.

The first lens is the economic argument itself. Hyperbolic growth stories usually rest on a feedback loop: more output lets you produce more of the key inputs to growth, and those inputs feed back into more output. Historically the bottleneck was that ideas come from people, and population can only grow so fast. The worry, or the hope depending on your perspective, is that if AI systems can substitute for human labor across essentially all of the tasks that matter for producing goods and especially for doing research, then you've removed that bottleneck. So the question I'm really asking is less "how impressive is this model" and more "what fraction of economically and scientifically relevant tasks can AI do as well as, or better and more cheaply than, a human?" And importantly, it's about the tail. Automating 90% of tasks might give you a big boost, but if the remaining 10% are real bottlenecks, they can dominate, a Baumol-style effect. Growth gets limited by whatever you still can't automate.

The second lens is looking at trends in capabilities and in what goes into them: compute, algorithmic progress, data. You can try to extrapolate when systems reach some threshold of generality. I take those extrapolations seriously, but I hold them loosely, because the mapping from benchmark performance to "can actually do the job" is pretty noisy. Models can look superhuman on a test and still fail at the messy, long-horizon, context-heavy work that real jobs involve.

So the third lens, which I think is increasingly the most informative, is watching for real-world signals. Are AI systems doing tasks autonomously over longer and longer time horizons? Are they actually speeding up AI research itself? That one matters a lot, because AI accelerating AI development is the most direct version of the feedback loop. Are firms reorganizing around them, rather than just using them as a productivity aid for humans?

I'd also flag that even if the capabilities are there, there are frictions: physical-world bottlenecks, regulation, the time it takes to build factories and run experiments, adoption lags. Those could slow the transition from "AI can do this" to "the economy is growing hyperbolically." I don't think they stop it indefinitely, but they matter for timing.

So the short version: I'm looking for broad, robust automation of tasks, especially research tasks, plus evidence of the feedback loop closing, rather than any single capability milestone.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't have a clean metric, and I'm pretty suspicious of anyone who says they do. But let me try to say what I actually look at.

The thing that would drive hyperbolic growth, in the sort of standard economic story, is AI being able to substitute for human labor across basically the whole range of tasks that go into making the economy bigger, including the task of making AI itself better. So the question I'm really asking is not "how impressive is this model on a benchmark" but "how much of the actual work is it doing end to end, without a human in the loop fixing things?"

And those come apart a lot. You can have a system that scores extremely well on, say, a coding benchmark, and then you watch it try to complete a multi-week project in a real codebase and it falls over for reasons that have nothing to do with the benchmark. It loses track of what it's doing, it doesn't notice that it's made an error three steps back, it can't handle the parts of the task that involve going and asking someone what they actually meant. So one thing I pay a lot of attention to is the length and messiness of tasks that models can reliably complete autonomously. METR has done some nice work trying to measure the time horizon of tasks that models can do, and watching how fast that's growing is, I think, one of the more informative signals we have. Not because the number itself is sacred, but because the trend tells you something about whether the gap between "impressive demo" and "actually does the job" is closing.

The second thing I look at is whether AI is meaningfully accelerating AI research. This is the feedback loop that matters most for the hyperbolic story. And here I try to be pretty concrete: are researchers at labs actually getting substantially more done than they were a year ago, and is that attributable to AI tools rather than just to more compute or more people? My sense at the moment is that the answer is "somewhat," particularly for engineering work, but it's not yet the case that the models are generating the research ideas or running the research program. When that starts happening in a way that people inside labs can't dismiss, I'd update quite a bit.

Third, I look at diffusion into the broader economy, and I try to separate adoption from impact. Lots of companies say they're using AI. Far fewer can point to a specific measurable change in their output. The hyperbolic growth story requires the latter, at scale, and it also requires that the bottlenecks that aren't about intelligence, like physical infrastructure, regulation, building things in the real world, don't just reassert themselves and slow everything down. I think people who are very confident about hyperbolic growth often underweight how much of the economy is not cognitive labor, or at least is not cognitive labor that can be sped up without also speeding up a bunch of physical processes.

And then the last thing, which is more of a meta point: I try to notice when I'm reasoning from the capabilities I find most salient rather than from the ones that actually matter economically. It's very easy to be impressed by a model doing something I personally find hard, like a tricky math problem, and to extrapolate from that. But the economy doesn't care whether the thing is hard for me. It cares whether the thing is a bottleneck, and whether removing it actually lets you do more. So I try to keep asking: if this capability were perfect tomorrow, what would actually change? Sometimes the answer is "a lot," and sometimes it's "honestly, not that much, because the hard part was never the thing the model is now good at."

So putting that together, I'd say I'm looking for sustained, autonomous completion of long, messy tasks, clear evidence that AI is substantively driving AI progress, and measurable rather than reported impact in the broader economy. I don't think we're at the point where hyperbolic growth is obviously underway. I also wouldn't be shocked if we got there in a small number of years, which I realize is an uncomfortable combination. But I think the right response to that is to watch those specific indicators closely rather than to pick a confident story and defend it.

r001.rationale: It calls AI-driven progress in AI research the feedback loop that matters most and says whether models begin generating research ideas would substantially change the speaker’s assessment.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes strong coding benchmark performance and AI-assisted engineering from the more consequential threshold of generating research ideas, indicating coding ability alone is insufficient.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether AI can substantially automate the process of making further technological progress, particularly progress in AI itself. It’s not enough for a model to be impressive on a benchmark. You want to know whether giving it more compute actually lets you get more research done, without needing a proportional increase in human supervision.

So I’d look for systems that can take a research problem, come up with hypotheses, run experiments, interpret the results, and use those results to decide what to try next. And then I’d ask what’s still bottlenecked on humans or on physical infrastructure. If you can make the software better very quickly, but you have to wait years to build the chips it needs, that matters a lot.

The reason this could produce hyperbolic growth is that better AI could let you do research faster, which gives you better AI, which lets you do research faster still. But whether that feedback loop actually leads to accelerating growth depends on how strong it is relative to diminishing returns and those bottlenecks. So I’d put more weight on evidence that AI is speeding up the whole research process than on any particular capability milestone.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look at how much AI can accelerate the process of developing better AI. There’s a potential feedback loop: better AI makes research faster, which gives you better AI, which makes research faster again. But the existence of that loop isn’t enough to establish hyperbolic growth. You need to know how strong it is and what bottlenecks remain.

So I’d be more interested in AI systems carrying out substantial research projects than in their scores on individual benchmarks. Can they choose useful experiments, run them, interpret the results, and turn those results into improvements? And does that actually shorten the time it takes to produce the next generation of systems?

You’d also want to account for things like compute, chip production, and the time required to run experiments. Even if the intellectual work becomes much faster, those constraints could matter a lot. So I don’t think there’s a single capability threshold where I’d say, ‘Okay, now we should expect hyperbolic growth.’ I’d want evidence that the feedback loop is getting stronger across the whole process.
